Incremental mediated elasticity: the P_med^delta curve

Source: vignettes/incremental-pmed.qmd

Why a curve, not a number

The standard proportion mediated Pmed=IIE/OEP_{med} = \text{IIE} / \text{OE} answers the question “what share of the effect passes through the mediator?” for one fixed contrast A=0A = 0 vs A=1A = 1. But that contrast is arbitrary when treatment is a continuous or graded dose. The incremental mediated elasticity replaces the global contrast with a derivative question: if assignment odds are tilted by a factor δ\delta, what fraction of the resulting marginal shift in the outcome travels through the mediator?

Formally, the tilted assignment probability is

qδ(C)=δg(C)δg(C)+1−g(C),g(C)=P(A=1∣C), q_\delta(C) = \frac{\delta \, g(C)}{\delta \, g(C) + 1 - g(C)}, \qquad g(C) = P(A = 1 \mid C),

and the estimand is

Pmedδ(δ)=θmed′(δ)θtot′(δ), P_{med}^\delta(\delta) = \frac{\theta'_{med}(\delta)}{\theta'_{tot}(\delta)},

where θdir′\theta'_{dir} and θmed′\theta'_{med} are the marginal (derivative-scale) direct and mediated elasticities, and θtot′=θdir′+θmed′\theta'_{tot} = \theta'_{dir} + \theta'_{med} is their exact sum (no interaction remainder R(δ)=0R(\delta) = 0 for all δ\delta). The curve Pmedδ(δ)P_{med}^\delta(\delta) is the quantity that varies with δ\delta: it is flat under a linear-Gaussian model with no A×MA \times M interaction, and it bends — revealing the interaction — when one is present.

A worked example

The DGP below places an A×MA \times M interaction in the outcome so the curve is non-flat. incr_pmed() evaluates the estimand at five tilt values and returns an IncrPmedResult whose print method displays one row per δ\delta.

library(probmed)
n <- 1500
C <- rnorm(n)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.2 + 0.8 * C))
M <- 0.6 * A + 0.4 * C + rnorm(n)
Y <- 0.5 * A + 0.7 * M + 0.5 * A * M + 0.3 * C + rnorm(n)   # A*M interaction
d <- data.frame(A, M, Y, C)
fit <- incr_pmed(d, deltas = c(1/3, 1/2, 1, 2, 3))
fit
#> Incremental mediated elasticity P_med^delta(delta) (onestep-crossfit, n=1500)
#>   delta=0.333  P_med=0.490  [0.404, 0.577]  (dir=0.288 med=0.276 tot=0.564)
#>   delta=0.5    P_med=0.494  [0.415, 0.574]  (dir=0.223 med=0.218 tot=0.441)
#>   delta=1      P_med=0.501  [0.428, 0.573]  (dir=0.129 med=0.130 tot=0.259)
#>   delta=2      P_med=0.505  [0.436, 0.575]  (dir=0.065 med=0.067 tot=0.132)
#>   delta=3      P_med=0.507  [0.438, 0.577]  (dir=0.041 med=0.042 tot=0.083)

Each row of the printed table gives the mediated elasticity (med), total elasticity (tot), and PmedδP_{med}^\delta with its confidence interval at the corresponding δ\delta. Because the interaction term amplifies the mediated share as δ\delta grows (larger tilts assign more treated units and the A×MA \times M term compounds), the curve rises rather than remaining flat. A flat curve — constant Pmed across δ\delta — certifies that no interaction is present and the classical proportion mediated tells the whole story. A bending curve tells you that the “share through the mediator” depends on how aggressively you shift treatment, which a single number would obscure.

Inference

The estimator behind each row is a cross-fitted one-step (Kennedy 2019). The propensity score g(C)g(C) is fitted in cross-fitting folds and the pseudo-outcomes are constructed to be Neyman-orthogonal in gg: the influence function includes the full g-score (Kennedy 2019, Corollary 2, Term II). Orthogonality in the propensity means that first-order errors in ĝ\hat g do not inflate the asymptotic variance of the elasticity estimates — inference remains valid at standard nonparametric rates even when gg is estimated by a flexible learner.

Note carefully what orthogonality does not imply: because PmedδP_{med}^\delta is itself a functional of gg (the tilt qδq_\delta is a transformation of gg), double robustness of the point estimate is impossible (Kennedy 2019, §3.3). Misspecifying gg biases q̂δ\hat q_\delta, which biases the elasticity estimates. The efficiency and inferential robustness that orthogonality buys are genuine; DR of the point estimate is not on offer for this estimand, and probmed does not claim it.

Pointwise confidence intervals at each δ\delta are computed via the ratio-identity influence function for med/tot\text{med} / \text{tot}. Intervals are printed as [lo, hi] at the ci_level stored in the result object (default 95 %).

Sensitivity to M–Y confounding

Unmeasured confounding between the mediator and outcome is the canonical threat to mediation conclusions. incr_sensitivity() applies the additive-offset sensitivity model of pmed_sensitivity() to every row of the curve: it reports, for each δ\delta, the M–Y bias magnitude that would drive PmedδP_{med}^\delta to zero.

incr_sensitivity(fit, threshold = 0)
#>       delta        med        tot      Pmed     tipping tipping_threshold
#> 1 0.3333333 0.27643023 0.56394258 0.4901744 -0.27643023       -0.27643023
#> 2 0.5000000 0.21822093 0.44135523 0.4944338 -0.21822093       -0.21822093
#> 3 1.0000000 0.12968367 0.25906367 0.5005861 -0.12968367       -0.12968367
#> 4 2.0000000 0.06667354 0.13193290 0.5053594 -0.06667354       -0.06667354
#> 5 3.0000000 0.04224607 0.08331181 0.5070838 -0.04224607       -0.04224607

The column tipping is −θmed′(δ)-\theta'_{med}(\delta) — the additive numerator bias that would make the mediated share vanish at this δ\delta. tipping_threshold gives the corresponding quantity for the user-supplied threshold (here 0, so both columns coincide). Larger |tipping| at a given δ\delta signals that the mediated share at that tilt is more durable to unmeasured M–Y confounding. When the curve rises (as here, due to the interaction), the rows at large δ\delta typically have the largest absolute tipping values, meaning the interaction-driven amplification is also the hardest to explain away.

Summary

  • incr_pmed() estimates the incremental mediated elasticity curve Pmedδ(δ)P_{med}^\delta(\delta) at a user-supplied grid of tilt factors.
  • A flat curve signals no A×MA \times M interaction; a bending curve reveals one.
  • Inference is Neyman-orthogonal in the propensity but not doubly-robust in the point estimate (the estimand is itself a functional of gg).
  • incr_sensitivity() extends the curve object with per-δ\delta tipping-point analyses for M–Y unmeasured confounding.
